say: One company sold tiny slices of itself, for one hundred and thirty-five dollars each.
It raised seventy-five billion dollars.
In three days, the stock jumped two-thirds.
Then, it lost over half its value.
This is the story of the SpaceX I.P.O., the biggest the world had ever seen.
And the wildest part? The next giants are already lining up.
Imagine a company is a giant pizza.
Every share is one tiny slice.
For twenty-four years, SpaceX only sold its slices to a private club: founders, employees, and big investors.
Everyone else was stuck behind the rope.
An I.P.O., or initial public offering, is the day the doors swing open.
The company sells slices to anyone, on a public stock market, like the Nasdaq.
Initial: it's the first time.
Public: anyone can buy.
Offering: the company is selling.
So why would a company open its doors at all?
Reason one: money. Selling new slices brings in cash to build things.
Reason two: the private club finally gets a way to sell, too.
That's called cashing out.
And SpaceX needed a lot of cash.
For its rockets, its Starlink satellites, and, after merging with Elon Musk's A.I. company, ex A.I., in February, giant A.I. computers.
In twenty twenty-five, it brought in about eighteen point seven billion dollars, but still lost nearly five billion.
Think of a lemonade stand that sells a lot of lemonade, but spends even more building a giant new factory.
Building the future is expensive.
Going public is like launching a rocket. There's a countdown.
Step one: the paperwork.
SpaceX sent the regulator, the S.E.C., a secret draft on April first.
On May twentieth, it made that document public.
It's called an S-one, and it's basically the company's diary: what it earns, what it owes, and what could go wrong.
And anyone can read it for free, on the S.E.C.'s website.
Step two: the roadshow.
Starting June fourth, SpaceX and its banks pitched the stock to huge investors.
The lead banks were Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.
Banks like these are called underwriters. They organize the sale, and find the buyers.
For that work, the banks get paid a fee: a small slice of the money raised.
Step three: the order book.
Investors write down how many slices they want, and at what price.
Normally, a company names a price range. If the book overflows, the price can rise.
SpaceX skipped the range, and named one fixed price: one hundred and thirty-five dollars a share.
Even so, big investors asked for about four times more shares than there were.
Step four: pricing night. On June eleventh, the deal was locked in.
SpaceX sold about five hundred and fifty-six million new shares.
One hundred and thirty-five dollars, times five hundred and fifty-six million, is about seventy-five billion dollars.
The old record belonged to Saudi Aramco: about twenty-nine billion dollars, in twenty nineteen.
SpaceX's deal was more than two and a half times bigger.
And this time, regular people got a real seat at the table.
Usually, everyday investors get five to ten percent of an I.P.O.
SpaceX planned up to thirty percent, and in the end gave about a fifth to retail buyers, through apps like Robinhood, Fidelity, and Schwab.
There was one more trick: the greenshoe.
It lets the banks sell fifteen percent extra shares, if demand is hot.
Demand was hot. The banks used it, and the total grew to about eighty-five point seven billion dollars.
One more detail matters for later: Elon Musk kept about four-fifths of the votes.
The public could own slices, but Elon still picks the toppings.
June twelfth, twenty twenty-six. The opening bell.
S.P.C.X. opened at one hundred and fifty dollars, already above the I.P.O. price.
It climbed as high as one hundred and seventy-six dollars that day, and closed at one sixty point nine five, up nineteen percent.
That made SpaceX worth over two trillion dollars.
Headlines called Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.
A first-day jump like this is called an I.P.O. pop.
Why does it happen? The I.P.O. price is set before trading starts.
If more people want the stock than there are shares to sell, buyers bid the price up.
Some say a big pop means the company left money on the table.
In other words, maybe it sold its slices too cheaply.
But the rocket kept climbing.
On June sixteenth, just the third day of trading, S.P.C.X. touched two hundred and twenty-five dollars and sixty-four cents.
That's two-thirds above the I.P.O. price, in three trading days.
Early buyers felt like geniuses.
And then, gravity showed up.
Stocks rarely fall for just one reason. S.P.C.X. was pulled down by four weights.
Weight number one: the Cursor deal.
On the same day as the peak, SpaceX agreed to buy the A.I. coding company Cursor for sixty billion dollars, paid in stock.
Paying in stock means cutting new slices from the same pizza.
Every existing slice gets a little smaller. That's called dilution.
Within two trading days, SpaceX lost more than six hundred billion dollars in market value.
Weight number two: the lock-up.
Insiders who owned shares before the I.P.O. usually can't sell them for months.
It's a promise that stops everyone from rushing for the exit on day one.
SpaceX's first big unlock was set for August sixth: about nine hundred and eleven million shares.
That was almost seven percent of all SpaceX shares.
Worried about a flood of selling, investors pushed the price down ahead of time.
On July twenty-seventh, the stock hit a record low, under one hundred and nine dollars.
The funny part? On unlock day itself, the stock actually rose six percent.
And over the next five trading days, it climbed about thirty-five percent.
The fear did more damage than the flood.
Weight number three: spending.
In August, SpaceX handed in its first report card as a public company.
Revenue grew ninety-two percent, to seven point eight billion dollars. Great!
But it spent eighteen point four billion dollars in a single quarter, most of it on A.I.
That's money for giant computer chips and data centers, the kind that power A.I. models.
Investors hate surprise bills. The next day, the stock fell more than ten percent.
Just before that report, on August third, S.P.C.X. had touched its all-time low: one hundred and four dollars and eighty-three cents.
From the peak, that's a fall of about fifty-three percent.
Weight number four: the price tag itself.
At over two trillion dollars, buyers were paying for a future of Mars trips and space data centers.
When a price assumes everything goes right, any bad news hurts more.
It's like a rocket made of glass: beautiful, but one small pebble can crack it.
And there was a hidden risk: in the third quarter, one A.I. customer made up more than a third of revenue.
Bloomberg reported that customer is Anthropic, and the contract can be canceled with ninety days' notice from early twenty twenty-seven.
To be fair, the business kept growing.
In October, revenue jumped one hundred and sixty-one percent, and SpaceX made a four point four billion dollar profit.
The stock bounced. But by late November, it was back below its one hundred and thirty-five dollar I.P.O. price.
A great company and a great stock are not always the same thing.
Remember the queue at the launch pad? The next giants are taking off.
On November eighteenth, Anthropic, the A.I. company behind Claude, priced its I.P.O. at eighty-three dollars a share.
It raised eighty-one point three billion dollars, more than SpaceX's original seventy-five.
Its shares jumped on day one, then slid back toward the I.P.O. price within days. Sound familiar?
So is SpaceX still the biggest I.P.O. ever? It depends how you count.
Count SpaceX's greenshoe, and its eighty-five point seven billion is still bigger, at least for now.
Count only the starting deal, and Anthropic wins.
Next in line: Open A.I., the maker of Chat G.P.T.
It has reportedly filed in secret, and is aiming for twenty twenty-seven, with reported valuations above one trillion dollars.
And other big private companies, like Databricks and Stripe, are often named as future candidates, with no dates set.
So what can the SpaceX story teach us, before the next mega I.P.O.?
One: a first-day pop is not a promise.
Two: check the lock-up calendar. More SpaceX shares unlock on December eighth.
Three: watch for dilution. New slices make your slice smaller.
Four: read the S-one diary, especially the part about what could go wrong.
And five: a famous name doesn't make the price cheap.
SpaceX is still building rockets, satellites, and A.I. computers.
Whether its stock reaches Mars is a different story.
Because in the stock market, just like in space, what goes up has to fight gravity.
This video is for education, not financial advice.
